lessons.title: Saying Hello and Goodbye
lessons.body:
In Shona, greetings change depending on the time of day and whether you're addressing one person or a group. Start with the most common: "Mhoro" (hello) for one person, "Mhoroi" for multiple people or to show respect. In the morning, say "Mangwanani" (good morning). Around midday, use "Masikati" (good afternoon). In the evening, "Manheru" (good evening). For goodbye, "Chisarai" means "stay well" to those remaining, and "Fambai zvakanaka" means "go well" to those leaving. If you're the one leaving, say "Ndichaona" (I'll see you) or simply "Sara zvakanaka" (stay well).

Practice these with a partner. For example, greet a neighbor in the morning: "Mangwanani, mama. Wakadii zvako?" (Good morning, mother. How are you?). She might reply, "Ndiripo, wakadiiwo?" (I'm fine, how are you?). Use "Mhoroi" when entering a shop or meeting a group of elders. In rural areas like Chivi or Bindura, it's polite to greet everyone before stating your business. A simple "Mhoroi" to all present shows respect.

When leaving, if you're the visitor, say "Ndichaona" or "Fambai zvakanaka" to those staying. If you're staying, say "Chisarai" or "Sara zvakanaka" to those leaving. Listen to how locals say it: often they add the person's name or title, like "Chisarai, baba" (Stay well, father). Tone mattersâkeep it warm and unhurried. In Zimbabwe, a handshake or a slight bow accompanies greetings, especially with elders. Women may kneel or clap hands lightly as a sign of respect in traditional settings.

To master these, use them daily. Greet your family in the morning with "Mangwanani" and at night with "Manheru". When you leave a room, say "Ndichaona" to those remaining. Practice with a friend: one leaves, the other stays, and switch roles. Record yourself to check pronunciation. The more you use these phrases, the more natural they become. Remember, Shona greetings are not just words; they are a bridge to community. Start every interaction with a greetingâit opens doors and shows you value the other person.

lessons.title: Asking and Giving Names
lessons.body:
Asking and giving names in Shona is straightforward but comes with cultural nuances. To ask "What is your name?" say "Unonzi ani?" (literally "You are called who?"). For a group, use "Munonzi ani?" If you want to ask a child, you might say "Wanonzi ani?" The response is "Ndinonzi..." (I am called...). For example, "Ndinonzi Tendai." If you want to ask for someone's surname, say "Zita rako ndiani?" or more commonly "Unonzi ani?" covers both. To ask "What is his/her name?" say "Anonzi ani?" For "What are their names?" use "Vanonzi ani?"

When giving your name, you can simply say "Ndinonzi [name]." If you want to be formal, say "Zita rangu ndi [name]" (My name is [name]). In Zimbabwe, people often have a Shona name and an English name. For example, "Ndinonzi Tapiwa, asi kuchikoro ndinonzi Peter." (I am called Tapiwa, but at school I am called Peter.) It's common to ask "Unogara kupi?" (Where do you stay?) after names. To respond, say "Ndinogara kuHarare" (I stay in Harare).

Practice with a partner: Ask "Unonzi ani?" and answer. Then ask about origin: "Unobva kupi?" (Where are you from?) and answer "Ndinobva kuMasvingo." Use these in real situations. When you meet someone new at a market in Mbare, start with a greeting, then ask their name. Listen carefully to their response and repeat it back to show you heard. If you forget, say "Ndapota, unonzi ani zvakare?" (Please, what is your name again?). This shows effort and respect.

To remember, create flashcards with questions on one side and answers on the other. Practice with a friend, taking turns. Use names of famous Zimbabweans: "Ndinonzi Morgan Tsvangirai" or "Ndinonzi Strive Masiyiwa." But in real life, use your own name. Also learn to ask about other people: "Anonzi ani?" (What is his/her name?) and "Vanonzi ani?" (What are their names?). When you introduce someone, say "Uyu ndi [name]" (This is [name]) or "Ava ndi [name]" (These are [name]). For example, "Uyu ndi Tafadzwa, shamwari yangu." (This is Tafadzwa, my friend.) Practice these phrases until they roll off your tongue.

lessons.title: Basic Polite Expressions
lessons.body:
Politeness is central to Shona culture. The most important expressions are "Ndapota" (please), "Ndatenda" or "Ndinotenda" (thank you), and "Pamusoroi" (excuse me/sorry). Use "Ndapota" when making a request: "Ndapota, ndipewo mvura." (Please give me water.) "Ndatenda" is used for thanks, often with a handshake or clap. If someone helps you, say "Ndatenda zvikuru" (Thank you very much). For apologies, "Ndineurombo" means "I'm sorry" (for a mistake), while "Pamusoroi" is for getting attention or excusing yourself. When passing by someone, say "Pamusoroi" to be polite.

Other useful phrases: "Makadii" (How are you?) is a polite greeting, and the response is "Ndiripo" (I'm fine). To say "You're welcome," use "Tisazve" or "Zvakanaka." If you don't understand, say "Handisi kunzwisisa" (I don't understand) or "Ndapota, taura zvishoma" (Please speak slowly). To ask for something, use "Ndinoda..." (I want...) but always add "ndapota." For example, "Ndinoda kuziva zita rako, ndapota." (I want to know your name, please.) When someone sneezes, say "Mwari akuropafadze" (God bless you). When someone is going to work, say "Shanda zvakanaka" (Work well). When they return, "Mauya" (Welcome back).

Practice these in daily interactions. At a shop in Bulawayo, say "Ndapota, ndinoda kutsvaga chingwa." (Please, I want to look for bread.) The shopkeeper might say "Hona henyu" (Here you are). Respond with "Ndatenda." If you bump into someone, say "Pamusoroi." If you arrive late, say "Ndineurombo nekunonoka." (I'm sorry for being late.) Use "Mhoroi" when entering a room, and "Ndatenda" when leaving. In rural areas, when you visit a homestead, clap hands lightly and say "Mhoroi" or "Makadii" before stating your business. This shows respect.

To remember, role-play with a friend: one asks for something, the other gives and receives thanks. Practice apologizing and responding. Use these phrases in real life as much as possible. For example, when buying airtime at Econet, say "Ndapota, ndinoda airtime yemadhora mashanu." (Please, I want airtime for five dollars.) Then say "Ndatenda" when done. The more you use them, the more natural they become. Politeness opens doors in Zimbabweâit shows you value others and their culture.

lessons.title: Introducing Yourself and Others
lessons.body:
Introducing yourself in Shona involves more than just saying your name. Start with a greeting: "Mhoroi" or "Mangwanani." Then say your name: "Ndinonzi [name]." Add where you're from: "Ndinobva ku [place]." For example, "Mhoroi, ndinonzi Rudo. Ndinobva kuMutare." If you want to say what you do, say "Ndinoshanda ku [workplace]" or "Ndirikudzidza ku [school]." For instance, "Ndinoshanda kuCBZ Bank." To ask someone else to introduce themselves, say "Ndapota, muzvitaurirewo." (Please introduce yourself.) Or simply "Unonzi ani? Unobva kupi?"

When introducing others, use "Uyu ndi [name]" for one person, "Ava ndi [name]" for multiple or respect. For example, "Uyu ndi baba vangu, VaMoyo." (This is my father, Mr. Moyo.) "Ava ndi vana vangu." (These are my children.) To introduce a friend, say "Uyu ishamwari yangu, Tinashe." (This is my friend, Tinashe.) If you want to say "He/She is from...", use "Anobva ku..." For example, "Anobva kuGweru." To say "They are from...", use "Vanobva ku..."

In a group, it's polite to introduce yourself first before asking others. At a community meeting in Kuwadzana, you might stand and say: "Mhoroi mose. Ndinonzi Farai. Ndinobva kuChitungwiza. Ndinoshanda nekanzuru." (Hello everyone. I am called Farai. I am from Chitungwiza. I work with the council.) Then others will follow. When introducing a visitor, say "Uyu ndi muenzi wedu kubva kuSouth Africa. Anonzi Thabo." (This is our guest from South Africa. He is called Thabo.) Always use titles for elders: "Sekuru" (grandfather), "Mbuya" (grandmother), "Baba" (father), "Amai" (mother). For example, "Uyu ndi Sekuru Moyo."

Practice with a friend: Take turns introducing yourselves with name, origin, and occupation. Then introduce each other to a third person. Use a mirror to practice your posture and gestures. In Zimbabwe, a handshake accompanies introductions, and you might hold your right forearm with your left hand as a sign of respect. For women, a slight curtsy or kneeling may be appropriate when greeting elders. Practice these introductions until you can do them without hesitation. The more you introduce yourself, the more confident you'll become. Remember, a good introduction includes a smile and eye contact.

lessons.title: Responding to Greetings
lessons.body:
Responding correctly to Shona greetings is key to smooth communication. When someone says "Mangwanani" (Good morning), reply "Mangwanani" or "Mangwanani, wakadii?" (Good morning, how are you?). If they ask "Wakadii?" (How are you?), the standard response is "Ndiripo" (I'm fine) or "Ndiripo, wakadiiwo?" (I'm fine, how are you?). For "Makadii?" (How are you? to an elder or group), respond "Tiripo" (We are fine) or "Ndiripo." When someone says "Mhoro" (Hello), you can reply "Mhoro" or "Mhoroi" if they are older or multiple. If greeted with "Masikati" (Good afternoon), reply "Masikati" or "Masikati, makadii?" (Good afternoon, how are you?).

Other common greetings and responses: "Wakadii zvenyu?" (How are you? formal) â "Ndiripo zvenyu." "Mauya" (Welcome back) â "Ndauya" (I have come) or "Ndatenda." "Uri kupi?" (Where are you?) â "Ndiri pamba" (I'm at home). "Uri kuita sei?" (How are you doing?) â "Ndiri kuita zvakanaka" (I'm doing well). If someone says "Ndatenda" (Thank you), respond "Tisazve" or "Zvakanaka" (You're welcome). If they apologize with "Ndineurombo," reply "Zvakanaka" or "Hazvina mhosva" (It's okay). When someone says "Chisarai" (Stay well) as they leave, respond "Fambai zvakanaka" (Go well) if you're staying, or "Chisarai" if you're also leaving. If they say "Ndichaona" (I'll see you), reply "Ndichaona" or "Zvakanaka."

Practice these responses in context. For example, at a bus stop in Harare, someone says "Mangwanani, wakadii?" You reply "Ndiripo, wakadiiwo?" Then they might say "Ndiripowo." If you're at a funeral, greetings are more subdued: "Mhoroi" or "Makadii" with a soft voice, and responses are "Tiripo" or "Ndiripo." In a business setting, use formal greetings: "Mangwanani, makadii zvenyu?" and respond "Ndiripo zvenyu, makadiiwo?" Always match the tone and formality. If someone greets you in a hurry, respond briefly but politely.

To master responses, practice with a partner. One greets, the other responds, then switch. Use different times of day and situations. Record yourself to check pronunciation and tone. Listen to Shona radio stations like Star FM or Radio Zimbabwe to hear natural responses. The more you practice, the more automatic they become. Remember, responding promptly and warmly shows respect and builds relationships. In Zimbabwe, a greeting is not just a formalityâit's a way of acknowledging the other person's humanity.

lessons.title: Cultural Norms in Greetings
lessons.body:
Shona greetings are deeply embedded in cultural norms that vary by age, gender, and setting. In rural areas, when you approach a homestead, you clap your hands lightly and say "Mhoroi" or "Makadii" before entering. This clapping, called "kukwazisa," is a sign of respect, especially to elders. Men usually clap with hands cupped, while women may kneel or curtsy. In urban areas like Harare, a handshake is common, but still show deference to elders by using both hands or holding your right forearm with your left. When greeting a group, greet the eldest first, then others. Never rush a greetingâtake time to ask about family and health.

Gender norms also play a role. In traditional settings, women may kneel when greeting men or elders, and men may not extend a hand to a woman unless she offers first. However, this is changing in cities. When greeting a chief or headman, you may need to remove your hat and clap while bowing slightly. In some areas, you say "Mambo" (Chief) or "Ishe" (Lord) as a title. At funerals, greetings are subdued: "Mhoroi" or "Makadii" with a soft voice, and you may say "Ndineurombo" (I'm sorry) to the bereaved. At weddings, greetings are joyful and may include ululation.

Time of day matters: "Mangwanani" until about 10 a.m., "Masikati" until around 4 p.m., and "Manheru" after that. But in practice, people often use "Mhoro" or "Makadii" throughout the day. When leaving, it's polite to say goodbye to everyone individually, especially elders. If you're visiting, say "Ndatenda nekuuya" (Thank you for coming) to your hosts. If you're the host, say "Mauya" (Welcome) and offer water or food. In business, greetings are still importantâstart meetings with a round of greetings before discussing agenda.

To navigate these norms, observe locals. When in doubt, be respectful and ask. For example, "Ndapota, ndinofanira kuita sei kukwazisa vanhu vakuru?" (Please, how should I greet elders?). Practice in real situations: at a market, greet the vendor before asking prices. At a church, greet the pastor with "Mhoroi, Mufundisi." At a rural home, clap and wait to be invited in. Learn from mistakesâif you forget to clap, apologize. The key is sincerity. Shona people appreciate effort to respect their customs. Over time, these norms become second nature, and you'll build deeper connections.

quiz.q: What is the correct Shona greeting for 'Good morning'?
quiz.explanation: 'Mangwanani' is used in the morning, while 'Masikati' is afternoon and 'Manheru' is evening.

quiz.q: How do you say 'Hello' to a group of people in Shona?
quiz.explanation: 'Mhoroi' is the plural/respectful form of 'Mhoro' used for multiple people or to show respect.

quiz.q: What does 'Chisarai' mean?
quiz.explanation: 'Chisarai' means 'stay well' and is said to those remaining when you leave.

quiz.q: How do you ask 'What is your name?' in Shona?
quiz.explanation: 'Unonzi ani?' literally means 'You are called who?' and is used to ask someone's name.

quiz.q: What is the response to 'Unonzi ani?'
quiz.explanation: 'Ndinonzi...' means 'I am called...' and is the correct response to 'Unonzi ani?'.

quiz.q: How do you say 'Please' in Shona?
quiz.explanation: 'Ndapota' means 'please' and is used when making a request.

quiz.q: What does 'Ndatenda' mean?
quiz.explanation: 'Ndatenda' or 'Ndinotenda' means 'thank you' in Shona.

quiz.q: Which phrase means 'Excuse me' or 'Sorry' when getting attention?
quiz.explanation: 'Pamusoroi' is used to excuse oneself or get attention politely.

quiz.q: How do you introduce a friend in Shona?
quiz.explanation: 'Uyu ndi shamwari yangu' means 'This is my friend' and is used to introduce a friend.

quiz.q: What is the correct response to 'Makadii?' (How are you? to an elder)?
quiz.explanation: 'Tiripo' means 'We are fine' and is the respectful response to 'Makadii?'.

quiz.q: How do you say 'Goodbye' to someone who is leaving?
quiz.explanation: 'Fambai zvakanaka' means 'Go well' and is said to someone who is leaving.

quiz.q: What does 'Ndineurombo' mean?
quiz.explanation: 'Ndineurombo' means 'I'm sorry' and is used to apologize for a mistake.

quiz.q: How do you ask 'Where are you from?' in Shona?
quiz.explanation: 'Unobva kupi?' means 'Where are you from?' and is used to ask about origin.

quiz.q: What is the response to 'Mauya' (Welcome back)?
quiz.explanation: 'Ndauya' means 'I have come' and is the correct response to 'Mauya'.

quiz.q: Which greeting is used in the evening?
quiz.explanation: 'Manheru' means 'Good evening' and is used in the evening.

quiz.q: How do you say 'You're welcome' in Shona?
quiz.explanation: 'Tisazve' or 'Zvakanaka' means 'You're welcome' in response to thanks.

quiz.q: What is the polite way to greet an elder in a rural area?
options: B) Clap hands lightly and say 'Mhoroi'
quiz.explanation: In rural areas, clapping hands lightly and saying 'Mhoroi' shows respect to elders.

quiz.q: How do you ask 'What is his/her name?' in Shona?
quiz.explanation: 'Anonzi ani?' means 'What is his/her name?' and is used for one person.

quiz.q: What does 'Ndiripo' mean?
quiz.explanation: 'Ndiripo' means 'I'm fine' and is a common response to 'Wakadii?'.

quiz.q: Which phrase means 'Please speak slowly'?
quiz.explanation: 'Ndapota, taura zvishoma' means 'Please speak slowly' and is useful when learning.

quiz.q: How do you introduce yourself formally in Shona?
quiz.explanation: 'Zita rangu ndi...' means 'My name is...' and is a formal way to introduce yourself.

quiz.q: What is the response to 'Ndatenda' (Thank you)?
quiz.explanation: 'Tisazve' or 'Zvakanaka' is the polite response to 'Ndatenda'.

quiz.q: How do you say 'Good afternoon' in Shona?
quiz.explanation: 'Masikati' means 'Good afternoon' and is used around midday.

quiz.q: What does 'Ndichaona' mean?
quiz.explanation: 'Ndichaona' means 'I'll see you' and is used when leaving.

quiz.q: Which phrase is used to apologize for being late?
quiz.explanation: 'Ndineurombo nekunonoka' means 'I'm sorry for being late' and is a specific apology.

quiz.q: How do you ask 'How are you?' to a peer?
quiz.explanation: 'Wakadii?' is used to ask 'How are you?' to a peer or someone younger.

quiz.q: What is the response to 'Wakadii?'?
quiz.explanation: 'Ndiripo' means 'I'm fine' and is the correct response to 'Wakadii?'.

quiz.q: How do you say 'Welcome' to a guest?
quiz.explanation: 'Mauya' means 'Welcome' and is said to a guest upon arrival.

quiz.q: What is the title for 'grandfather' in Shona?
quiz.explanation: 'Sekuru' means 'grandfather' and is used as a respectful title.

quiz.q: Which phrase means 'It's okay' in response to an apology?
quiz.explanation: 'Zvakanaka' means 'It's okay' and is used to accept an apology.
